CausalChain: Dietary and probiotic interventions → modulate gut microbiota composition → enhance bile salt hydrolase and bile acid transformation enzymes → increase conversion of primary bile acids to UDCA → elevated physiological levels of UDCA lead to selective activation of tumor-suppressive nuclear receptor pathways (e.g., FXR/PXR) and inhibition of NF-κB/MAPK signaling → reduced epithelial-mesenchymal transition and cell proliferation in colorectal epithelium → decreased risk of colorectal carcinogenesis.
Hypothesis: Altering the gut microbiome to enhance endogenous production of UDCA will rebalance bile acid signaling in the colon, thereby suppressing pro-inflammatory and proliferative pathways to reduce the initiation and progression of colorectal cancer.
Abstract: Bile acids, known primarily for their roles in lipid digestion and cholesterol homeostasis, are increasingly recognized as key signaling molecules influencing carcinogenesis via interactions with nuclear and membrane receptors. Recent evidence indicates that bile acids can exert both tumor‐promoting and tumor‐suppressing effects in a concentration‐dependent and tissue‐specific manner. Notably, ursodeoxycholic acid (UDCA) demonstrates potent antitumor actions in several gastrointestinal cancers, whereas other hydrophobic bile acids such as deoxycholic acid (DCA) may promote carcinogenesis through activation of proliferative and inflammatory pathways. Moreover, the gut microbiota plays a decisive role in determining the composition of the bile acid pool through enzymatic transformations. Building on this, we propose a novel hypothesis that targeted modulation of the gut microbial community can shift bile acid metabolism to favor UDCA production, enabling the suppression of oncogenic signaling pathways in colorectal tissues.
